title: A Patrol Cutter
text: The same cutter drifts up on your quarter like a neighbor. "Well, hello again," Osei says. "You answered so nicely last time that I've been telling people about it." "Now, a small thing, and I'd ask it of anyone." The petty officer is off the band for once, and Osei's voice is the only one. "Sam. Who signed Sam on, and where? The dock, I mean. I'm fond of docks. I grew up above one, and the sound of the lift still gets me in the mornings." Osei laughs, softly, at nothing. "The name of whoever put a pen to it, and the berth number if you have it. That's all. It's not a trap, and I'd tell you if it were. I'm terrible at keeping those."
labels: Answer it, and shade one detail (then keeping quiet at the stop is less likely to see them through)

plays.text: You answer, and Osei listens to the whole of it without a sound, which is its own sort of attention. When it's done there's a small warm noise on the band, a sort of hum. "That's lovely," Osei says. "You'd be surprised how many ships get that wrong, in either direction." The petty officer says something off-band, and Osei says, "No, they're fine," in the voice of someone settling a bet. "Right," Osei says. "The crew list, since we're here. I'll go through it nice and slow, like grace before a meal, and we'll all be away in time for tea."

title: A Patrol Cutter
text: The same cutter drifts up on your quarter like a neighbor. "Well, hello again," Osei says. "Last time one of your answers was a little off, and you were so pleasant about it. I remember pleasant." "Now, a small thing, and I'd ask it of anyone." The petty officer is off the band for once, and Osei's voice is the only one. "Sam. Who signed Sam on, and where? The dock, I mean. I'm fond of docks. I grew up above one, and the sound of the lift still gets me in the mornings." Osei laughs, softly, at nothing. "The name of whoever put a pen to it, and the berth number if you have it. That's all. It's not a trap, and I'd tell you if it were. I'm terrible at keeping those."
labels: Answer it, and shade one detail (then keeping quiet at the stop is less likely to see them through)
Answer with "Who's asking?" [60%; if it fails: the stop goes worse, and the captain marks it]

plays.text: You answer, and Osei listens to the whole of it without a sound, which is its own sort of attention. When it's done there's a small warm noise on the band, a sort of hum. "That's lovely," Osei says. "You'd be surprised how many ships get that wrong, in either direction." The petty officer says something off-band, and Osei says, "No, they're fine," in the voice of someone settling a bet. "Right," Osei says. "The crew list, since we're here. I'll go through it nice and slow, like grace before a meal, and we'll all be away in time for tea."

next.title: A Patrol Cutter
next.text: The list reaches Sam Vale, and Osei slows by a single beat, the way a hand slows at a bad rung. "This one is wanted by the Compact," Osei says, and waits. On your deck nobody is looking at Sam, with such care that it amounts to looking. The cutter hasn't moved. Its lock is stowed, and the ticking on the band is its drive keeping pace with yours, which is what a ship does when it means to stay. In the back of the call the petty officer's pen has stopped. You have a few seconds in which the whole next hour belongs to you, and you can feel exactly how few.

title: A Patrol Cutter
text: The same cutter drifts up on your quarter like a neighbor. "Well, hello again," Osei says. "Last time you asked who was asking, and I went and told the whole mess. They still laugh." "Now, a small thing, and I'd ask it of anyone." The petty officer is off the band for once, and Osei's voice is the only one. "Sam. Who signed Sam on, and where? The dock, I mean. I'm fond of docks. I grew up above one, and the sound of the lift still gets me in the mornings." Osei laughs, softly, at nothing. "The name of whoever put a pen to it, and the berth number if you have it. That's all. It's not a trap, and I'd tell you if it were. I'm terrible at keeping those."

title: A Patrol Cutter
text: The same cutter drifts up on your quarter like a neighbor. "Well, hello again," Osei says. "Last time you asked who was asking. I wasn't offended. I'm told I should have been." "Now, a small thing, and I'd ask it of anyone." The petty officer is off the band for once, and Osei's voice is the only one. "Sam. Who signed Sam on, and where? The dock, I mean. I'm fond of docks. I grew up above one, and the sound of the lift still gets me in the mornings." Osei laughs, softly, at nothing. "The name of whoever put a pen to it, and the berth number if you have it. That's all. It's not a trap, and I'd tell you if it were. I'm terrible at keeping those."
labels: Answer it, and shade one detail (then keeping quiet at the stop is less likely to see them through)
Answer with "Who's asking?" [60%; if it fails: the stop goes worse, and the captain marks it]

plays.text: You answer, and Varga reads it back to you, word for word, slowly enough that you can hear how it sounds in someone else's voice. It sounds fine. "Thank you," Varga says. "That is consistent with the register." The pen stops, which you hadn't noticed it doing until it did. The frigate closes to fifty kilometers, with no hurry and no menace, the way a door closes. "Now the crew list, please," Varga says. "I will read it aloud, and you will tell me if any name is mispronounced. It is a courtesy. Please do not take it as an invitation."

title: A Patrol Cutter
text: The Concord frigate holds a hundred kilometers off and speaks first, which is correct procedure, and the officer who speaks is correct about everything else too. "Commander Varga, Dome Concord, aboard the frigate," the voice says. "Thank you for matching. The crew list will wait one moment, and I would be obliged for a complete answer." A pen scratches somewhere behind the voice. "Who signed Sam onto your articles, and at which dock? The name, please, and the dock." Varga waits, and you can hear the pen waiting too. "I write what's said to me," Varga says, "exactly as it's said. Please bear that in mind."
labels: Answer it, and shade one detail (then keeping quiet at the stop is less likely to see them through)
Answer with "Who's asking?" [60%; if it fails: the stop goes worse, and the captain marks it]

plays.text: You answer, and Varga reads it back to you, word for word, slowly enough that you can hear how it sounds in someone else's voice. It sounds fine. "Thank you," Varga says. "That is consistent with the register." The pen stops, which you hadn't noticed it doing until it did. The frigate closes to fifty kilometers, with no hurry and no menace, the way a door closes. "Now the crew list, please," Varga says. "I will read it aloud, and you will tell me if any name is mispronounced. It is a courtesy. Please do not take it as an invitation."

title: A Patrol Cutter
text: Varga is on the band again, at the same distance, with the same pen. "Dome Concord remembers you," Varga says. "Last time you answered everything I asked, in order. Thank you. Today I'll ask something different." The pen is already moving. "Your articles, please, and the date of your last landing. The date, and the dock." Somewhere behind Varga a second voice reads a number from a screen, and Varga says, "Thank you, not yet." The frigate hasn't moved closer, and doesn't need to. "I will read your answer back to you," Varga says, "so that we both hear it. If a word is wrong, now is the moment to say so. It is a courtesy, and it is only offered the once."

plays.text: You answer, and Varga reads it back to you, word for word, slowly enough that you can hear how it sounds in someone else's voice. It sounds fine. "Thank you," Varga says. text: It's Teague again, on the same band, with the same collar and a new slate. "We've met," Teague says. "You had it right last time, so I'll ask something else." The petty officer in the background leans over a screen. "Cargo seals. Read me the numbers off your hold, bow to stern, and don't go and look them up." title: A Patrol Cutter
text: It's Teague again, on the same band, with the same collar and a new slate. "We've met," Teague says. "Last time one of your answers was off. I looked it up. So this time I'll ask something I can check faster." The petty officer in the background leans over a screen. "Cargo seals. Read me the numbers off your hold, bow to stern, and don't go and look them up." You can hear the cutter ticking as it matches your thrust. "Last ship that read me seals off a manifest had two of them reversed," Teague says. "The crew list is next, either way. I'd just like to know what kind of ship I'm reading it to." The pen is out. It's the same pen.

title: A Patrol Cutter
text: It's Teague again, on the same band, with the same collar and a new slate. "We've met," Teague says. "Last time you asked who was asking. I said it twice. I won't say it a third time, so I'll just ask something else." The petty officer in the background leans over a screen. "Cargo seals. Read me the numbers off your hold, bow to stern, and don't go and look them up." You can hear the cutter ticking as it matches your thrust. "Last ship that read me seals off a manifest had two of them reversed," Teague says. "The crew list is next, either way. I'd just like to know what kind of ship I'm reading it to." The pen is out. It's the same pen.

plays.text: Halfway through a docking run into a station berth the intercom clicks, and the engineer asks whether somebody is running the sim off the main bus again, because the coolant pumps can hear it. "We are," Ines says, without taking her eyes off your board. "Ten more minutes." "Five." "Ten. Then you can have your bus back." The intercom clicks off. "Where were we. You're fast, and you'll stay fast unless you watch the number." You bring the closure rate down to the number and hold it there to the berth, and she doesn't reset it. At ten minutes she shuts the sim down and calls the engine room to say so. (+3 experience at the pilot post.)
mem: 10 Jul 2214: We spent some downtime together.

plays.text: Tomas has the pressure log open on the engine room bench and has you read it out, line by line, while he listens to the loop with his head on one side. At the sixth line he stops you. "Once more." You read it again. "That's not her. That's the gauge." He taps the glass, and the needle drops a tenth. "Write the real number. Put a G next to it." You put a G next to it. Four lines up there is another G in his hand, and two pages back, three more. "I've asked for a new gauge at every port," he says, and turns the page. (+3 experience at the engineer post.)

plays.text: Yelena bets you a dessert ration on one set of forty targets on the range sim, best total wins. Thirty, she says, is for children. Through the first half she calls the Ravens' old plays at her own targets, by number. When your total passes hers on the board she stops calling them. You finish three short. "Three," she says, and holds out her hand for the ration chit. She folds it once and tucks it into the strap of her knee brace. (+3 experience at the gunner post.)

plays.text: There's a callsign in the stack that Ruben stops at and doesn't put on any pile. "That's my kitchen," he says. "Was. The relay we ran in the strike. Somebody's still using the call." He reads the intercept to the bottom and laughs once, short. "They've got the timing wrong. We sent on the half hour." It goes into his shirt pocket instead of a pile, and he finds the call's frequency on the console and leaves it up. "On the half hour, key it once. Three seconds, no message. Write down the time." You key it at the half hour and write down the time. By the end of the watch nothing has come back, and he has you write that down too, under it. (+3 experience at the comms post.)

plays.text: Ines loads a bad approach into the sim and gives you the left seat: a crosswind at the pad and a vector from the tower that's ninety seconds stale. You fly it into the deck. "You flared," she says, before the board has finished going red. "Stop first. Then flare." She resets it. On the second run she hums with her eyes shut and corrects you twice without opening them, once aloud and once by tapping the throttle with one finger. The third goes into the deck as well, and she resets it without a word. The sixth comes down inside the numbers, and she writes the time in her logbook. "Tomorrow, same hour," she says, already unstrapping. "I'll make the tower lie both ways." (+3 experience at the pilot post.)

plays.text: Tomas takes you down the coolant loop on a slow watch, valve by valve, with the engine room door propped open. She likes the air, he says. To the pipes he talks low, in Igbo, and doesn't stop. To you he gives each valve's name and what it's for, and nothing else, until the fourth, where he takes your hand and puts it flat on the line beside his. "Feel that? Pump. The bearing's behind it." He takes the hand back. "When you can feel the bearing, come and get me." He holds out the spanner handle-first. "Quarter turn. Properly." You turn it a quarter. The pipe over your head ticks twice and settles. (+3 experience at the engineer post.)
mem: 11 Jul 2214: We spent some downtime together.

plays.text: Yelena runs the range sim with the ring-ball feed up on the second screen, the Olympus Ravens two down at the half, and she coaches both. "Not there. Where the next pass goes," she says to you, and to the Ravens' keeper, at the same volume, "Where are you going? Where is he going? Look at him!" She shoots her own set left-handed, to make it fair, and gets four of five. The fifth she swears at until the sim resets. When the Ravens score she stands up, and sits down again rubbing the knee. You hit three of your last five. "Better," she says, without looking around. They lose by one. She turns the feed off. "Referee's from Hellas," she says, and runs your set again from the top. (+3 experience at the gunner post.)
mem: 11 Jul 2214: We spent some downtime together.

plays.text: Ruben hands you a thermos and half a stack of intercepts, and the two of you sort them at the console into three piles, which he labels TRUE, FALSE and LOVELY on strips of tape. TRUE gets two all watch. He talks the whole time. "This one says Hellas is short of filters. Hellas is short of filters every time they lose a tech, and they lost two in June." He holds it up to the light. "Dated the first of June. They lost the second tech on the ninth. Somebody ordered the filters before they needed them." It goes on LOVELY. He shows you the tells: a timestamp in the wrong decade, a callsign that's too polite. By the end of the watch LOVELY is the taller pile. Ruben squares it with both hands and starts on the second half of the stack. (+3 experience at the comms post.)
mem: 11 Jul 2214: We spent some downtime together.

plays.text: Bexa takes you down to the hold to rig the tether winch on a crate, the way she'd rig it on a hatch. She shows you the hitch the Ceres tugs use, which the manual calls wrong. "Manual's never towed anything." She hands you her old tug gloves, two sizes too big and stiff at the knuckles, and you tie it in those. "Nobody ties one bare outside." Your third hitch holds under the winch's full pull. Your fourth jams the drum. Bexa looks at it, then at the clock. "Leave it," she says. "It'll still be jammed when you've slept." (+3 experience at the pilot post.)
mem: 11 Jul 2214: We spent some downtime together.

plays.text: Pax sets up the range sim, and the two of you take turns calling the numbers to each other: the range, and the second the charge is hot. On Pax's turns the numbers are perfect, and on the first three Pax flinches when the round goes. "Sorry. Sorry. It's not you," Pax says, to the screen. By the halfway mark the apologies have stopped, though the flinch hasn't, and the numbers come quicker. At the end Pax sits back and looks at the rail housing on the diagram. "What does it actually do in there? When it fires. Has anybody ever opened one up?" Pax is already out of the seat. "The engineer will know." (+3 experience at the gunner post.)
mem: 11 Jul 2214: We spent some downtime together.

plays.text: You cook something real out of the good stores: garlic, rice in the pressure pot, and the block of butter that has been missing a corner for a week. "Who had the butter?" "Nobody had the butter." "The butter has teeth marks." Everyone off watch comes to the galley, which seats five, and the rest eat standing with bowls passed over shoulders. The engineer eats in the doorway with one foot in the corridor, in case. Seconds run out before the last two get any, and the crust in the pot goes to whoever has the next watch.
mem: 9 Jul 2214: The captain shared a meal with us.

plays.text: You call a breach in the hold, and the drill says the hold gets sealed with whoever is in it, and you are in it. The door closes on you. Through the port you watch them work the corridor side, a sheet of foam going on the frame and someone on the intercom reading the gauge to the bridge: "Ninety-eight. Still ninety-eight." You wait by the door the way the drill says to wait, suit sealed, while the hold's own gauge reads full the whole time. At six minutes the door opens, and the first one through checks your suit seals before saying anything. (Better odds in a fight for the rest of this burn.)

A pass through a dust stream left the cable conduit along the spine pitted for twenty meters, and you spend the watch on it a meter at a time: cut the bad run out, splice it, sleeve it, tape the sleeve. The splices want a steady hand, and the spine flexes every time the recycler cycles, so you time each crimp to the gap between its thumps. Hull 40 to 50 of 50. You test every splice twice, on the way down the spine and on the way back. The third from the aft end reads low both times, and you cut it out and do it again.

You make the rounds of the berths, knocking on each door in turn and waiting for the closer to cycle. You hear out a complaint about the air recycler, a story about a cousin on Ganymede who won a boat at cards and lost it by the following week, and a request for an extra blanket, which you've got. From one passenger, the quiet one in the end berth, you get a question: whether it's normal to feel this far from everything. You promise to look into the recycler. You tell them it is.
mem: 9 Jul 2214: The captain came to check on us.

plays.text: You run the flip drill on the sim: cut the drive, swing the ship end over end, and light it again on the new heading, smoothly enough that nothing loose aboard moves. That is what the sim scores. The first flip puts a tool roll and two bulbs of coffee into the air on the sim's deck plan. After that most of the ship stays put, and the sim flags the restart as two seconds late every time. (+3 experience at the pilot post.)

You spend a watch on the range sim, tracking and leading targets: two hundred rounds, the first sixty of them spent on where the target was. The sim gives you a score and a lane-by-lane breakdown. Your worst lane is the curved one, which is the one a real raider takes. (+3 experience at the gunner post.)

You go through the plant one system at a time, with the manual open on your knee and a meter in your teeth, and find two things nobody wrote down: a gauge that reads four percent high, and a bracket held on by habit. You pencil them inside the cover of the manual, under the last note in the margin, which is dated eleven years ago. (+3 experience at the engineer post.)

You sit on the bands for a watch, learning the rhythm of a dozen stations: who comes up on the hour, who stays on after the tower has told them to clear, who reads the weather slowly enough to be copied by hand. You learn which of them lie about their transponders by the way a callsign drifts a digit when the traffic is thin. You log four, and a fifth at the end of the watch. (+3 experience at the comms post.)
The captain has the magazine filled at the yard, 2 bought for 8,000 cr from the ship's fund.
There's nothing to practice.

Tomas walks you aft to the coolant loop behind the guns and opens the cover on the bleed valve with his thumbnail. "This dumps the heat off every gun into the radiators at once, and the locks come off with it." He hands you the valve key, handle first and has you turn it twice with the loop cold. Then he tells the loop, "I know, I know, you hate it, and it's once a fight and no more, and I'll have you topped up again before anyone shoots at us."

title: Settling Up
text:
The ramp is down. Cato has the captain's notebook open on a crate on the apron, and he turns it round so you can read it. "She's at the harbor office. I'm to show you the page and bring it back."

40 t of water, bought for 20,000 and sold for 31,000: the ship clears 11,000. The captain had it down for 9,000.
Your pay: 1,200 in wages for 9 days, less 0 for your kit.
The hiring hall takes 30 percent of your pay, 800. You still owe it 39,200.

"My first share was nine hundred," he says. "I bought boots with it. They were the wrong boots, and I wore them for six years." He taps the page. "Yours is in your account. It's in your savings."

There is a column for the officers' shares, with Tomas and Ines in it. The ratings are paid by the day, and your name is on the wage page. "That column's Hester's," Cato says. The pencil stays behind his ear.

"You're off until Hester has a plan. The Missions page has day jobs on the station, and that pay is yours. Anything farther off, you put to the captain. The bar has people in it who are not crew."

plays.text:
He starts at the galley. "We eat here and we argue here, mostly at the same time. The galley's on the rota, same as everything, and your turn's on the board. The water ration's on the wall in chalk. Don't rub it out."

In the hold he slows down. "That's Hana," he says, nodding at the deckhand lashing a cargo pod. "You'll get asked to hold a strap. Hold it, and don't let go until you're told." He checks the lashing himself anyway.

The engine room is warm and the deck hums under your boots. "Tomas's plant. Don't touch anything with a tag on it, and everything has a tag." Up forward he points at the bridge without going in. "Ines flies her. If you have the bridge watch, Ines comes up for the flip. Don't talk during the checklist." Beside the bridge, Mateo has the relay. "Your messages come through Mateo, in the batch, twice a day."

At a row of doors on the left he stops. "Third one is yours. It's on a closer, so it hisses, it doesn't slam. You'll try to slam it once. Everyone does."

The last stop is at the foot of the guns. "And these are yours. When something closes on us, the board shows you what she's about to do and what the captain means to do back. You lay a gun on a part of her, her guns, say, or her drive, and you press Fire, and then it all happens at once, hers and ours. You'll get one wrong. I did, and I'm still here, and so is the ship."

He takes the pencil from behind his ear and checks the rota. "That's everyone. You're on the middle watch. If you're hurt, come to me. I hold the first-aid kit, and I'd rather see you early than late." He writes your name on the back of his hand, in case the rota goes missing.
"Fair enough," Cato says. "The rota's on the galley wall. Everything else you'll find by walking into it, and I'll be somewhere nearby when you do." He tucks the rota back under his arm.

title: Third Approach

plays.text: You say nothing, and she doesn't go over. She finishes her drink and puts the glass down. "Not tonight," she says. On the way out she nods to him, once, and he nods back.

title: The Bartender Who Listens
text: Ruben Castellanos has made a friend of the bartender, or the bartender of him. plays.text: You walk over and say you work with a man who knows more about the dome network than anyone alive. The councillor goes still. "Castellanos," she says. "The relay in the kitchen." title: The Council Member

title: At the Reactor
text: The reactor alarm is a rising note that you feel in the deck before you hear it. The coolant loop has lost pressure, and the board shows the pile heating faster than the pumps can carry it. Ilsa is already at the shielded door, pulling on gloves. "There's a manual scram at the back of the housing," she says. "I know where it is. Nobody else does. Give me three minutes." She says it to the bridge, item by item. The plant is in good order. Cato has the med kit open at the door. The engineer is suiting up behind her. She waits for your answer, and has already started on the second glove.

title: The Fight She Shouldn't Have Picked
text: A ship has come up on your stern, long and dark, and it's one of Dobrescu's. Captain Pell has seen it on the board and is already at the guns, laughing, with a figure in her head. "We can take her," she says. "We could take her." Ansel is at the boarding lock with his coat on and the sheet in one hand. "I'd like to speak to them," he says. "Give me ten minutes, and the lock, and don't fire." He says it flat. Your hull is sound. Cato has the med kit open at the lock. Nobody else is on the guns. He waits for your answer, and has already put a hand on the lock.
labels: Back the captain, and open fire

plays.text: You tell her no, and call the go-round. The ship stands off from the gate, and the ice sits in the hold, and the cells burn for the second pass. Pilar takes her hands off the stick one at a time. "It's your call," she says. "It was always going to be somebody's."

title: The Docking Emergency
text: The gate's tractor beam fails twenty seconds out, and the ship is carrying forty tonnes of ice at a closing speed the berth was never meant for. The nav display is lagging. Captain Sato, on the bridge, has the checklist open. Pilar has the stick. "I can bring her in by hand," she says, "if you let me, and if you don't put anything on the display." title: Signing On
text:
The queue at the foot of the elevator is kept by the berth book, and a clerk won't stamp a book until the shifts owed on it are stood. Yours has two seasons of gate duty in it and no berth. The berths go to people with a cousin, and you have a trade and no cousin. The card was pinned to the notice board at the arcology docks, in pencil: HAND WANTED, ICE HAULER, DEPARTS WHEN FULL. The Iron Anvil, an ice hauler out of Earth, took you for what you could do. Captain Hester Vance reads your papers twice. The second time she has a pencil, and she writes your wage into a ruled notebook before she looks up. "500 a day, less your kit," she says. "That's the whole of it. I won't surprise you, and I'd like you not to surprise me."

You have the helm: Captain Hester Vance plots the run, and you fly it, by hand.

Captain Hester Vance picks each run and carries freight for a shipper, who pays on delivery. Errands for wherever she's going come through the port, and the captain keeps a fifth. A hand who saves can have a ship of their own: the cheapest at a yard, a Dust Skiff, is 100,000 cr. Your papers name you a member of the Arcology Compact, and its officers read them, at customs and on patrol. Why did you sign on?

You grew up under the domes of Tharsis, where everyone argues about the future, and the Concord's navy didn't want you. You spent a winter learning how many ways a no can be worded. Then a freighter at Phobos Yards put out a call for a hand, and nobody asked about your politics, only whether you could stand a watch. The Iron Anvil, an ice hauler out of Mars, is yours to work. Captain Imre Sato reads your papers once, straight through, and writes the time on them. The jacket is navy, and has been worn for years without a mark on it. "650 a day, less your kit," they say. "The rules are on the wall of the galley. They apply to everyone, including me. Noted that you're aboard."

You have the guns. When a contact closes, you choose how to meet her, and the move at the guns is yours alone. Working beside you: Yelena Quint, ring-ball striker from Olympus Dome, on the pilot post, and Ruben Castellanos, dome network administrator from Valles Dome, on the comms post, and Pilar Quesada, the first officer, from Callao Arcology.

Captain Imre Sato picks each run and carries freight for a shipper, who pays on delivery. Errands for wherever she's going come through the port, and the captain keeps a fifth. A hand who saves can have a ship of their own: the cheapest at a yard, a Dust Skiff, is 100,000 cr. Your papers name you a member of the Dome Concord, and its officers read them, at customs and on patrol. Why did you sign on?

plays.text: The Concord offered you a dome stipend. The freighter offers 475 a day, 25 more than the first offer, in writing, and you read the page to the bottom before you sign.
The navy wouldn't teach you. On the first day you ask to see the coupling, and the engineer shows you, and then has you do it.
The domes will argue about the future without you. Aboard, nobody asks whose side you're on. The first thing anyone asks is whether you have eaten.

plays.text: You find Captain Vance at the suit lockers, hanging up a suit somebody stowed wet, and you ask. The captain doesn't turn around. "Ask me something you'd need on the bridge with a contact closing." You do. The captain gets the suit onto its hook and answers it, short, then has you ask it again, faster, and answers it again, shorter. "Like that. If I'm wrong up there, tell me at that speed." The captain shuts the locker on the wet suit and takes the drip tray forward to empty it. (+2 experience at the gunner post.)
mem: 10 Jul 2214: You asked me for advice.

plays.text: An hour into your watch beside Mate1, a warning comes up amber on the pilot board. Mate1 reads it and goes to stand by the hatch. "I'm not here." You find the fault in the post's manual on the side screen and work it down, and the amber goes out at the ninth step, eleven minutes in. Mate1 comes back, reads the board's record through all nine steps standing up, and copies the eleven minutes into the post's log with your name beside them. (+3 experience at the pilot post.)
mem: 10 Jul 2214: You spent a watch at my post to learn it.

plays.text: Mate2 hands you a helmet lamp that cuts out whenever it's tilted, and tilts it to show you. "Every time I look down at a bolt." You take it apart on the lid of a ration tin and find a hair across the contact. You put the lens back on. Mate2 tilts the lamp at the deck ten times and it stays lit. 600 cr comes across, and Mate2 takes the hair away on a strip of tape, to show someone.
mem: 10 Jul 2214: You mended my gear.

plays.text: Two hours into the captain's watch a freighter hails and asks for the captain by name. You answer as the watch. "Then wake your captain," the freighter's mate says. "Nine thousand four hundred a ton to your next port, and it's good while I'm on this channel." The mate is off the channel before you've answered. At four the same freighter hails again, at eight thousand five hundred a ton, and asks for the captain by name again. 400 cr lands in your account at the next ledger sync. (+1 experience at the gunner post.)
mem: 10 Jul 2214: You stood a spare watch for me.

plays.text: Halfway down the gunner checklist, Mate2 stops you. "We did that one backward on my last ship. Faster." You have Mate2 show it. It's faster, and it skips a check, and the two of you argue it over the board until the coffee's gone and keep half of each. You write the new step into the post's checklist in your own hand, and Mate2 reads it over your shoulder and corrects the spelling. (+1 experience at the gunner post.)
mem: 10 Jul 2214: You spent a watch teaching me your post.

plays.text: Somebody puts a tin of real peaches, saved since the last port, in the middle of the galley table and calls it a prize, for the worst berth anyone ever slept in. A cargo net on a hauler. A bunk over a reactor housing that ticked all night. Two weeks in an escape pod. "That doesn't count." "It counts double." A closet at Tycho with a mop in it, which loses because the mop was clean. The crew vote by knocking on the table, two knocks a vote. The bunk over the reactor wins, and the winner eats the peaches out of the tin with a spoon, all of them, while the table watches.

plays.text: Captain Vance is at the galley table with a bulb of coffee gone cold, and pushes the other chair out with a boot when you sit down. "Years back, on someone else's ship," the captain says, "the first watch I had the deck. Shielding lashed for a two-g burn, and we ran at three, and I watched the straps go and logged it after the paperwork was in. Forty-two thousand for the cargo, and the late log cost me the berth." The bulb goes down on the table. "This run we're lashed for two-g, and we burn at one point eight." (+2 experience at the gunner post.)

plays.text: The rule at the pilot post is that you touch nothing, and for the first hour of the watch you touch nothing while Mate1 works. plays.text: You call a gun drill, only the guns, with training rounds and the sim for a target. The loaders race each other, and on the third pass one of them drops a round. It rolls the length of the bay and stops against the far rack, and nobody moves until the loader who dropped it walks over, turns it to the stencil and reads it out: "Inert." Someone laughs, and then all of them do, and the next pass is the fastest of the watch. The round goes back on the rack with a chalk mark on it. (Better odds in a fight for the rest of this burn.)

After the last hard burn the frame bolts want re-torquing, every one of them, and the torque wrench clicks at the number or it doesn't. You work along the ribs with a grease pencil, marking each bolt as it clicks. Four don't reach the number before the wrench slips, and you mark those with a circle. Hull 40 to 50 of 50. The four circles are still circles at the end of the watch. You leave them on the ribs for whoever has the wrench next, and put it back in the stores.

You call it, and the klaxon goes, and the whole ship comes off its bunks at once. Damage control first: the closers on the section doors, then a hose run out the length of the corridor to the galley. Then the guns, against the stopwatch, with somebody's boot caught in a deck tie-down and its owner hopping to the hatch. Then damage control again, because the watch said so, and an argument in the corridor over who left the galley hatch open on the drill fire. "It was a drill." "It was open." Four minutes ten, start to finish; the number on the card by the hatch is three-forty. When it's done the crew sit on the deck with their backs to the frame, breathing, and someone says, "Again at the flip," and gets no answer. (Better odds in a fight for the rest of this burn.)

You spend a watch crawling the frame with a heat gun and a tin of compound, filling old scars one plate at a time, the flashlight in your teeth. The worst is a seam by the aft lock that has wept since Ceres, and after it a dent in the cargo bay wall that nobody has owned up to. The compound takes forty minutes to set and smells of hot pennies. Hull 40 to 50 of 50. It's slow work, all of it yours, with no one to say whether the last seam is good. You sit against the wall with your hands black to the wrist until the compound stops smelling.

When it's done the crew sit on the deck with their backs to the frame, breathing, and someone says, "Again at the flip," and gets no answer. (Better odds in a fight for the rest of this burn.)

You spend a watch crawling the frame with a heat gun and a tin of compound, filling old scars one plate at a time, the flashlight in your teeth. The worst is a seam by the aft lock that has wept since Ceres, and after it a dent in the cargo bay wall that nobody has owned up to. The compound takes forty minutes to set and smells of hot pennies. Hull 40 to 50 of 50. Mate0 takes the seams you can't reach and does them with the plate off its hangers, in half the time, naming each one. When it's done Mate0 picks one bead off with a thumbnail and lays it again.

Mateo signs off at the dock office with one bag and leaves the rest to go on in the hold, tagged for the next port. Hana is on the corridor deck that night with a bucket, at the plate where the fight was. The new slicer, Chen, comes aboard with the hiring slip still in hand and has to step over the bucket.

title: Contact
text: Sensors: a drive plume at 3,420 km, on an intercept course. No transponder, and one plume, with nothing else on the board behind her. A raider who works alone picks a hauler with no escort, since one grapple crew can take a ship this size and nobody has to share. "Two guns on this ship, and she hasn't changed her line for either of them," Captain Vance says.

title: Contact
text: Sensors: a drive plume at 3,420 km, on an intercept course. A corsair, with her transponder off and her launcher bay open. On the open band she reads out the ship's name and the payment this ship is carrying, due on the first, and asks for it before the first comes. "Somebody at the last berth can count," Captain Vance says, and cuts the band.

title: Contact
text: Sensors: a drive plume at 3,420 km, on an intercept course. Transponder: Compact cutter, with a stop order for the ship's registry. Her hail reads it as a check of papers at the lock, and whatever is out of order on them is cited and fined from the ship's fund on the spot. A ship that burns away from a check is fired on, the hail says, and it says so twice.

title: Contact
text: Sensors: a drive plume at 3,420 km, on an intercept course. It's two raiders and not one, lying off the lane, and only the first has lit her drive. Word goes round a dock when a crew has been asking a yard about a hull, and the raiders who hear it hunt in pairs, one to pin the drive and one to board. The second plume lights as the first one turns.

title: Contact
text: Sensors: a drive plume at 3,420 km, on an intercept course. A corsair comes off the yard's own beacon with her drive already lit. Her hail names the Ore Runner and the price on the yard list, 170,000 cr. "The bank sells the names of who's asking after its ships, eighty credits a name," the voice says, "and yours was on it this week."

title: The Guns Hatch
text:
Cato is at the guns hatch before you have your boots on. He has the watch bill under his arm. "Look at the top of the board," he says. "That's what she means to do next, and under it what the captain will do with the helm. You don't guess either."

He points at the guns. "Each one goes where you send it: her guns, her drive, her lock, her hull. Then Fire, and you see what came of it. Take her lock and she can't board us. If she hits us hard, someone gets hurt, maybe you, and your work counts a level lower for some days. I had it in the hold. I wore a glove for eleven days."

He taps the gauge over the breech. "Every shot puts heat in the guns, and past that mark one locks for a turn. An overcharged shot hits harder and runs hotter. The turret up top fires with the guns, or you hold it back and it takes the edge off what she throws at us, torpedoes most of all. Holding it costs you a gun. When she opens her bay doors, you have one turn to choose. We carry a few torpedoes of our own. They hit hard, and when they're gone they're gone."

plays.text: The safety is where he said it would be. "Breathe out before you squeeze," Cato says. "Everyone forgets the first time."

title: The Inner Lock
text:
Cato has the sidearm locker open and hands you yours butt first. "Same as the guns," he says. "The top line's what they mean to do. The board's the deck, a box a section. Ours on the left, theirs on the right, and the dots are cover. Fewer dots, less to get behind."

He points at the line under it. "That's their count, and the mark is where they break. Put enough of them down and the rest go back the way they came. Each turn you stand or move a section, and you do one thing there. Then you give one of us an order. Me, if you like. I'll tell you if it's a bad one."

plays.text: You match velocity, and cross in suits, and find three people in the yacht's galley, gray-faced, wrapped in blankets, breathing in shallow sips. You patch their air recyclers with a borrowed part, and share some rations, and stay until the color returns to their cheeks. The owner, a rich man in a torn silk shirt, grips your hand so hard it hurts. "I won't forget this," he says.

next.title: The Owner
next.text: The owner, Halden Voss, has recovered enough to be embarrassed. He runs a shipping house out of Luna, he says, and the yacht was a present to himself. "Name your price," he says. "I'd rather it were a fair one. I'm told I'm a poor judge of my own life."
labels: Ask for a letter of introduction

nextPlays.text: He transfers it without looking at the number, and thanks you again, quietly, and then a third time.
He transfers it without looking at the number, and thanks you again, quietly, and then a third time.

He writes it on the back of his own business card, in a shaky hand, with a pen borrowed from your galley: "Bearer saved my life. Treat accordingly." He seals it with a thumbprint. "Don't lose it. I'll make sure the right people know."

"Nothing," you say. "Go home." He looks at you and doesn't answer at once. "Then I owe you something worse than money," he says. "I'll think of something."

plays.text: It was bait. Two raiders light their drives the moment you match velocity, dark shapes swinging out from behind the yacht's hull, guns already hot. The "life support failure" was a recording, looping on a dead panel. You break away, hard, with 78 points of armor damage and a long, ringing anger, at yourself, at them, at a universe in which this works.

next.title: They Follow You
next.text: The raiders aren't done. Two dark shapes keep pace off your quarter, closing, and the yacht behind them has gone from a distress call to a decoy to a joke. On the open band a voice you haven't heard before says: "Cargo or hull, friend." There's a pause.
labels: Burn hard to break away (30 reaction mass)

nextPlays.text: You throw the drive wide open, and the ship groans, and the two shapes fall behind, one at a time, still talking on the band, still cheerful about it. When the last of them is a spark, someone in the galley starts, shakily, to laugh.

You turn, and fire, and so do they, and the exchange is short and loud and ugly. You come out of it with the hull scarred and both raiders limping for the dark. The yacht's decoy transponder is still pinging from a lost position. You write it down. 52 points of armor damage.

You send the credits, and they take them, with a mock bow on the channel, and a "pleasure." They don't follow.

plays.text: You tune out the signal, and tell yourself it's probably a trap, and it probably is. It fades behind you, thinner and thinner, until it's just a whisper in the static, and then it stops. You don't sleep well, that night, and you don't know whether it's because of the voice or because of the silence that followed.

title: Distress Call
text: A signal cuts through the static: "...reactor scram... life support failing... anyone..." The voice is thin and cracked. A private yacht is drifting ballistic just off your trajectory, small and dark, with a single tumbling running light. There's no other traffic within a day's burn. Whoever is aboard hasn't much air left.
labels: Kill your burn and help (costs time)

plays.text: You transfer 5,000 cr. They peel off with a flash of their running lights, three long, one short, and on the open band a last, cheerful "Safe burn, hoser." You sit in the quiet with your hand still on the transfer key.

You jettison 10t of Water. The crates tumble away into the dark, spinning and glinting. The pirates chase them down, whooping on the channel, while you burn on. You watch their running lights dwindle, and try not to do the arithmetic.

{crew}'s fake transponder reads as one of their own, with a scrawled skull for good measure. They wave you through with a rude gesture, and one of them calls you "brother" over the channel. You don't answer. Your hands on the controls aren't steady.
They see through it in seconds and open fire. 52 points of armor damage before you get clear, and {crew} sits still afterward, mouthing a numbered list of what went wrong.

title: Pirates Matching Course
text: A dark ship with no transponder slides in off your quarter and matches your burn, close enough that you can see the scars on her hull, and paints you with targeting lidar, a cold red pulse across your instruments. A voice on the open band, amused and very young: "Cargo or credits, hoser. Your choice." Behind it, in the noise, someone's laughing, and someone else is quietly counting.
labels: Pay them off (10% of your credits)
Hard burn to outrun them (50 reaction mass)

plays.text: You go aboard in suits, through a tangle of cold, dark passages, past frozen coffee bulbs and a child's drawing pinned to a bulkhead, and cut out the nav core and a crate of spare parts, worth 29,000 cr to the right buyer. On the way out, you don't look at the drawing. You almost make it.

next.title: The Drawing
next.text: On the way out, the child's drawing comes with you, pinned to your sleeve by a bit of tape. Under the crayon, in careful adult handwriting, there's a ship name and a registry number.
labels: Put it in the log and say nothing

nextPlays.text: It takes an afternoon of slow channels and a favor from a registry clerk, but the name resolves, in the end, to a home and a family. You put the drawing in a drawer, and the drawer stays slightly open.

You tape it to the inside of a locker, and close the locker.

plays.text: Something in the reactor section was still live. A blue-white flash, a slam like a hammer, and the blast, as you scramble for the airlock, costs you 39 points of armor, and leaves your ears ringing for an hour. You don't go back for the parts. Nobody suggests it.

Whatever happened to them, it's not your business. You log the position, the ship's name and the time, and move on. Behind you the dead ship dwindles. Someone in the galley keeps watching the screen, and nobody says why.

title: Derelict Ship
text: Your sensors pick up a derelict drifting dark, an old ore hauler with her hull breached, her running lights out, and a long black scorch mark down one side. No transponder, no life signs, no heat signature. She has been dead a long time. Salvage rights go to whoever gets there first, and the cockpit has gone quiet.

plays.text: {crew} is in the coolant loop before the alarm finishes, sleeves rolled, one hand already on the valve. For twenty minutes there's only the sound of tools, and the hiss of venting steam, and low muttering. Then the lights go back to green, one by one. "Go back to sleep, captain," {crew} says, wiping their hands, black to the elbows.

An hour in a vac suit with a sealant gun and some swearing, wedged into a space the size of a coffin, with a flashlight in your teeth and a hot jet hissing at your elbow. Near the end of the hour the hiss stops. Good as new. You crawl out, drenched, and someone hands you a cup of tea without a word.

next.title: The Patch
next.text: The patch holds, but it's ugly: a lump of sealant the size of a fist, bulging over a section of pipe that's thinner than it should be. The drive is happy. The pipe isn't. A patch on a pipe like that doesn't last.
labels: Pay a yard to replace the section at the next port (4,000 cr)

nextPlays.text: You book it, and it's dull, and it works. The old section comes out in a yard worker's gloves, with the patch still on it, and the worker holds it up and says, with real admiration, "Whoever did this was brave."

You leave it, and it holds, day after day. Every watch someone puts a hand on the pipe.

plays.text: The patch fails, in a spray of hot white vapor, and you vent 50 units of reaction mass before you get it sealed, on the second try, with a great deal of swearing and a scorched sleeve. When it holds, at last, you slide down the wall and sit on the deck, laughing, because it's that or something else.

title: Coolant Leak
text: Alarms. A shrill wail goes through the whole ship, and on the reactor panel a line of lights goes from green to amber to red, one after another. The coolant loop has sprung a leak somewhere in the tangle of pipes behind the drive housing, and the drive is running hotter every minute, with a metallic ticking. The corridor smells of burnt glycol. Everyone's looking at you.
labels: Throttle back and burn extra mass to cool it

plays.text: {crew} pulls the drive apart, and puts it back together better, and takes most of a watch to do it. The burn runs ten seconds long, and the drive is at 60 percent.
{crew} pulls the drive apart, and puts it back together better, and takes most of a watch to do it. The burn runs ten seconds long, and the drive is at 60 percent.
It takes a borrowed tool kit and a great deal of swearing, but the drive comes back a little, to 42 percent. It will do.
You get the panel open and make it worse. The drive drops to 22 percent, and you close the panel quickly, as though nobody saw.
You decide to live with it. The drive slips a little further, to 26 percent, and everybody aboard learns to listen for it.

title: Drive Trouble
text: The drive has started to cough: a stutter in the thrust, and a rattle in the plume pipes that was not there before. It is at 30 percent and it will not get better by being ignored. The question is how much of the burn you are willing to spend on it.
